reasoning: The underlying PROBLEM — catching gradual/incremental sabotage that per-action monitoring can miss — is actively studied in the AI control literature, but via different mechanisms. The closest work (arXiv 2601.21112, "How does information access affect LLM monitors' ability to detect sabotage?"; ensemble/TraceGuard monitoring; CTRL-ALT-DECEIT) aggregates monitor suspiciousness via max-over-trajectory, averaging, or full-history monitors, and reports trajectory-level AUROC, while explicitly operating asynchronously/retrospectively and naming online mid-execution detection and detection-delay as unaddressed future work. CUSUM is itself a mature method (Page 1954) and has been applied to ML data-drift and even multi-agent norm change-point detection (arXiv 2512.18561), but no published work applies CUSUM sequential change-point detection to an AI-control monitor-signal stream and benchmarks detection delay versus a fixed per-action threshold under controlled drift rates. So the problem is partly covered but the specific method/framing (detection-delay-optimal sequential change-point detection on the monitor stream, evaluated on SHADE-Arena/ControlArena) is unexplored.

evidence.title: How does information access affect LLM monitors' ability to detect sabotage?
evidence.summary: AI-control monitoring paper. Monitors score full trajectories (AUROC at low FPR), with action-only vs CoT-only information access. Confirmed via fetch: does NOT use CUSUM or sequential change-point detection, no detection-delay analysis, no incremental/gradual sabotage accumulation; explicitly notes monitors operate asynchronously/retrospectively and that catching/interrupting agents mid-execution is desirable future work. Directly establishes the gap the proposal targets.

evidence.title: Ensemble Monitoring for AI Control: Diverse Signals Outweigh More Compute
evidence.summary: Aggregates monitor suspicion scores by arithmetic mean across monitors; thresholds calibrated to target FPR. Shows temporal aggregation across steps and spatial aggregation across monitors matter, but uses simple averaging/max rather than sequential change-point detection.

evidence.title: TraceGuard: Structured Multi-Dimensional Monitoring as a Collusion-Resistant Control Protocol
evidence.summary: Trajectory-level scoring uses max suspicion score per trajectory for attack-vs-honest ROC; per-action thresholds used for defer-to-trusted decisions. Represents current state-of-the-art aggregation (max / per-action threshold) that the proposal aims to outperform with CUSUM, but does not itself use sequential change-point detection or detection-delay metrics.

evidence.title: Adaptive Accountability in Networked MAS: Tracing and Mitigating Emergent Norms at Scale
evidence.summary: Treats norm detection in multi-agent systems as a sequential change-point problem, feeding diagnostic statistics into an adaptive CUSUM test tracking positive drift from baseline mean. Demonstrates CUSUM-for-agent-behavior is a known idea in MAS, but applied to emergent norms, not AI-control sabotage monitoring on benchmarks like SHADE-Arena/ControlArena.

evidence.title: A Note on Online Change Point Detection / CUSUM optimality (Page 1954)
evidence.summary: CUSUM is an established method, optimal in worst-mean-detection-delay sense for detecting abrupt distributional changes in sequential data. Confirms the proposed method is standard statistical-process-control machinery, so methodological novelty is low; the contribution rests on applying it to the AI-control monitor stream.

evidence.title: Out-of-Distribution Detection and Data Drift Monitoring using Statistical Process Control
evidence.summary: Applies SPC/CUSUM-style methods to ML data-drift/OOD monitoring, showing CUSUM beats per-point 3-sigma rules at catching gradual drift. Closely analogous methodology in ML monitoring but not in the adversarial AI-control sabotage setting; supports feasibility while showing the cross-domain transfer to control monitoring is the unexplored angle.
